title: Moving & Copying
description: Copy, move, and rename files and directories.

levels.title: Copying files — cp
levels.lesson:
`cp` (**copy**) duplicates a file. The original stays untouched.

```
cp source.txt destination.txt   # copy in the same dir (new name)
cp notes.txt Documents/         # copy INTO a directory
```

If the destination is an existing **directory**, the file lands inside it with its original name. If the destination is a **path that doesn't exist yet**, the copy gets that name.
levels.example:
$ cp notes.txt backup.txt
$ ls
.bashrc  Documents  Downloads  Desktop  notes.txt  backup.txt  projects

challenge.instruction: Copy `notes.txt` from your home directory into `Documents/` as `notes-backup.txt`.

levels.title: Copying directories — cp -r
levels.lesson:
Plain `cp` refuses to copy directories. Add `-r` (recursive) and it copies the entire directory tree:

```
cp -r projects projects-backup
```

The `-r` flag makes `cp` walk into subdirectories, copying each file, then each sub-directory.
levels.example:
$ cp -r projects projects-backup
$ ls
Documents  Downloads  Desktop  notes.txt  projects  projects-backup

challenge.instruction: Create a backup of your entire `projects` directory called `projects-backup` in your home directory.

levels.title: Moving files — mv
levels.lesson:
`mv` (**move**) does two things with one command:

1. **Move** a file or directory into a different location.
2. **Rename** it — by "moving" it to a new name in the same directory.

```
mv report.txt Documents/          # move to different dir
mv draft.txt final.txt            # rename in the same dir
mv Downloads/ archive/            # rename a whole directory
```

Unlike `cp`, the original disappears — there's only ever one copy.
levels.example:
$ mv notes.txt notes-old.txt
$ ls
.bashrc  Documents  Downloads  Desktop  notes-old.txt  projects

challenge.instruction: Rename the `Downloads` directory in your home directory to `downloads-archive`.

levels.title: Moving to a different location — mv
levels.lesson:
You can move a file across directories in a single `mv` command:

```
mv /home/user/notes.txt /home/user/Documents/
```

Or more conveniently with relative paths — just navigate to where you want to start and use `.` (here) and `..` (up one level):

```
cd /home/user
mv notes.txt Documents/
```
levels.example:
$ mv notes.txt Documents/notes-moved.txt
$ ls Documents
notes-moved.txt

challenge.instruction: Move `notes.txt` from `/home/user` into `Documents/` — it should end up at `/home/user/Documents/notes.txt`.

levels.title: Checkpoint — Moving & Copying
levels.lesson: Combine `cp`, `mv`, `mkdir`, and `rm` to reorganise a small file tree. Skills covered: `cp`, `cp -r`, `mv`, `mkdir`, `rm`.

challenge.instruction: Starting in `/home/user`: copy `notes.txt` into `Documents/notes-copy.txt`, then create a directory `archive` and move `Documents/notes-copy.txt` into it.
